name: Sight reading
description: Note-naming drills on treble, bass and grand staff: single notes and short passages, with key signatures, accidentals and playback. No instrument needed.

config.label: Reading tip
lines: Before you play or name anything: check the clef, then the key signature, then scan for the highest and lowest notes.
Treble clef lines, bottom to top: E G B D F (Every Good Boy Deserves Football). Spaces spell FACE.
Bass clef lines, bottom to top: G B D F A (Good Boys Do Fine Always). Spaces: A C E G (All Cows Eat Grass).
Learn a few landmark notes cold: middle C, treble G (the clef's curl), bass F (between the clef's two dots). Name everything else as a distance from a landmark.
Read by shape, not by name: a step is line-to-neighbouring-space, a third skips one, and so on. Your eye should see the interval before you name the note.
Ledger lines: count outward from the staff. The first ledger line above the treble staff is A; the first below is C (middle C).
Middle C sits on its own ledger line between the staves, one line below the treble staff and one above the bass staff.
In a key with sharps, the last sharp in the signature is a half step below the tonic. G major has F♯: every F is sharp until you see a natural.
In a key with flats, the second-to-last flat is the key. Two flats (B♭ E♭): B♭ major.
An accidental lasts until the end of the bar. A natural sign cancels the key signature for that note too.
Look ahead. While you name or play one note, your eyes should already be on the next two or three.
Don't stop to fix a mistake: keep the beat going and carry on, as you would in a real performance.
Check where the passage sits relative to the staff: is it mostly stepwise, or does it leap? Stepwise reading is faster; practise leaps separately.
Practise for a few minutes every day rather than long sessions: reading is a reflex you build with volume.
